source.title: Pre-interpolation loss behaviour in neural networks
source.citation: Arthur E. W. Venter et al., 2021
source.authors: Arthur E. W. Venter; Marthinus W. Theunissen; Marelie Hattingh Davel

record.tranche_reason: The study varies MLP capacity and training conditions and measures held-out loss and accuracy during training, using a different question and measurement from the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: No random-label experiment or direct comparison of test error across widths beyond the interpolation threshold. The reported results concern validation/evaluation loss and accuracy during training; related versions are not directly tested.
record.test_reason: The study measures divergence between held-out cross-entropy loss and classification accuracy during MLP training. Its width sweep compares training epochs within models, without reporting whether widening beyond the interpolation threshold lowers test error. It reports no direct comparison testing any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that sufficiently flexible MLPs can show increasing validation loss alongside stable or improving accuracy because extreme losses on specific examples dominate the average. They associate this with capacity, dataset size and difficulty, and increasing weight magnitudes, and recommend examining loss distributions. Concurrent fitting of generalizable and nongeneralizable features is their interpretation, rather than a direct random-label memorization result.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates validation loss and accuracy distributions during ordinary MLP training, rather than random-label memorization, width-dependent test error, or the other version-specific interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported phenomenon varies with model capacity, training-set size, dataset difficulty, and training conditions; FMNIST showed larger loss increases than MNIST, and larger models and smaller datasets showed the effect more often.

fits_no_version.finding: Average held-out cross-entropy can increase while classification accuracy remains stable or improves. The pattern is associated with greater model capacity, smaller training sets, and FMNIST rather than MNIST.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: During MLP training, rising average held-out loss can coexist with stable or improving held-out accuracy, with its occurrence depending on capacity and dataset conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Most held-out sample losses decrease while a minority become extreme; samples with extreme final validation losses generally remain outliers through much of training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A persistent minority of poorly modeled held-out examples can drive increasing average loss despite improving performance on most examples.

fits_no_version.finding: Some weight magnitudes increase at training iterations when extreme validation and evaluation losses increase.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing weight magnitudes temporally accompany worsening held-out losses for a minority of examples in the studied MLPs.

record.peer_reviewed: SACAIR; final authenticated publication stated as available online
record.problems: Small, focused investigation using only fully connected MLP classifiers on MNIST and FMNIST. Much of the evidence is qualitative and presented in plots; no uncertainty estimates are reported. Learning rates in the 80-model experiment were selected by validation error.

untested.parts: No fixed random-label experiment or comparison of natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy. Concurrent memorization and generalization are interpretive conclusions here.
No reported test-error trend across widths beyond the minimum width needed to interpolate; the measured contrasts are between epochs within models.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison or intervention on local connectivity.
Adam and SGD are used, but their relative held-out performance under controlled tuning is not reported.
Batch sizes vary, but no controlled large-versus-small-batch held-out performance comparison or adaptation experiment is reported.
Dropout is omitted rather than experimentally compared.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurements, generalization-gap correlations, or comparisons with alternative measures.
No memorization-influence estimation, training-example removal, retraining, or random-removal control.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to the listed versions, not a rejection of the study's separate findings. The supplied text does not provide readable cross-width accuracy values sufficient to turn R5 into a V2 test.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison with natural-label generalization.
No test-error sweep across widths beyond the width needed for zero training error; the paper studies validation loss and accuracy over training and across MLP settings.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
Adam and SGD are used in selected conditions, but the study does not compare their held-out generalization as an optimizer claim.
Batch sizes vary in some experiments, but no large-batch generalization-gap comparison is reported.
Dropout is omitted; its effect is not tested.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or comparison of generalization measures.

rows.subject: 95 two-layer MLPs
rows.size_stated: Hidden-layer width ranged from 7 to 2 000 nodes
rows.stage_stated: trained until interpolation (training accuracy of 100%), around 3 000 epochs for smaller models
rows.operation_detail: Varied hidden-layer width and optimizer over random initializations; compared validation metrics at their minimum-loss epoch and at first interpolation.

conditions.value: 3 per width for Adam; 2 per width for SGD

rows.baseline: Metrics at the epoch with minimum validation loss
rows.value: Larger models tended to show increases in both validation accuracy and loss, including before interpolation; limited-capacity models showed increasing loss and decreasing accuracy.
rows.note: Aggregate description of 95 models; the paper does not provide individual model values in the supplied text.
rows.check: The result concerns within-model changes from minimum validation loss to first interpolation. Although widths vary, no reported cross-width test-error trend establishes V2.

rows.subject: 80 MLPs
rows.size_stated: 1, 3, or 10 hidden layers; 100 or 1 000 nodes per layer
rows.operation_detail: Varied dataset, training-set size, depth, width, batch size, and optimizer; learning rates selected by grid search.

conditions.value: varied; sizes defined in Figure 3 legend

rows.baseline: Metrics at epoch with minimum validation loss
rows.value: FMNIST models tended to have much higher increases in validation loss while validation accuracy was still improving than MNIST models; models on MNIST or larger training sets generally had lower validation losses and higher validation accuracies.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative results for 80 models; exact individual values are not stated.
rows.check: The qualitative dataset comparison measures no claim version; 'partial' is therefore inappropriate. Specify the comparison endpoint: first interpolation where reached, or maximum training accuracy for models remaining below 100%, within the 150-epoch experiment.

rows.subject: Model A (3x100 MLP)
rows.size_stated: 3 hidden layers, 100 nodes per hidden layer
rows.stage_stated: trained until convergence; exact stopping criteria differ by experiment
rows.operation_detail: Measured per-sample loss distributions over training iterations.
rows.value: Loss decreased for a vast majority of samples, while a small minority had increasing loss; for validation and evaluation, those outlier losses seemed only to increase.
rows.note: The text characterizes the distributions qualitatively.
rows.check: Per-sample held-out loss distributions establish the study's separate phenomenon, not any listed version.

rows.subject: Model A (3x100 MLP)
rows.size_stated: 3 hidden layers, 100 nodes per hidden layer
rows.stage_stated: trained until convergence; exact stopping criteria differ by experiment
rows.operation_detail: Compared weight distributions with loss-distribution changes over training.
rows.measure: Weight magnitude distribution and validation/evaluation loss distributions
rows.value: Some weights increased in magnitude at the same iterations that validation and evaluation losses increased; this appeared more after most training-sample losses had been minimized.
rows.note: Authors describe an observed temporal correspondence, not a quantified causal effect.
rows.check: Weight magnitudes and their temporal correspondence with held-out losses are not magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness or its ranking of generalization gaps under V7.

rows.subject: Models A–D
rows.size_stated: 3 hidden layers, 100 nodes per hidden layer
rows.stage_stated: trained until convergence; exact stopping criteria differ by experiment
rows.operation_detail: Classified validation samples as outliers using the upper Tukey fence and tracked outlier epochs and final loss.
rows.measure: Persistence of validation-set outlier status and final sample loss
rows.value: End-of-training high-loss validation samples were usually outliers for most of training; a large majority were never outliers and ended with small loss.
rows.note: The supplied text gives the qualitative result; no per-sample numeric values are stated.
rows.check: Persistent high-loss validation examples are not training examples ranked by memorization influence and removed before retraining under V8.
